text: Rating Female Leaders
Herminia Ibarra and Otilia Obodaru present their research on attitudes towards female leaders in the workplace

runs.text: Herminia Ibarra and Otilia Obodaru present their research on attitudes towards female leaders in the workplace

text: Many believe that bias against women lingers in the business world, particularly when it comes to evaluating their leadership. Recently we had a chance to see whether this assumption was true. In a study of thousands of assessments collected by the executive education program of international business school Insead, we looked at whether women actually received lower ratings than men. Our research drew on evaluations of 2,816 executives from 149 countries enrolled in executive education courses at Insead. The managers filled out self-assessments and also invited subordinates, peers, supervisors, suppliers and consumers to evaluate them on a set of leadership dimensions. As we looked for patterns within this data, we focused on differences between the male and female leaders, both in terms of how they saw themselves and in terms of how the observers evaluated them.

As we looked for patterns within this data, we focused on differences between the male and female leaders, both in terms of how they saw themselves and in terms of how the observers evaluated them.

text: The first surprise for us, given prior published research, was that we found no evidence of a female ‘modesty effect’. Quite the opposite: Women rated themselves significantly higher than men rated themselves on four of the ten dimensions. Our analyses of how leaders were rated by their male and female associates – bosses, peers and subordinates – also challenged the common wisdom. Again, based on prior research, we had expected gender stereotypes to lower the ratings of female leaders, particularly those given by men. That was not the case. If there was a gender bias, it favored the female leaders: Male observers scored female leaders significantly higher than they scored male leaders on seven dimensions, and female observers scored them significantly higher on eight.

text: However, ratings on one dimension defied this pattern. Female leaders were rated significantly lower by their male and female superiors and male peers in ‘envisioning’ – the ability to recognize new opportunities and trends and develop a new strategic direction for an enterprise. This deficit casts a large shadow over what would otherwise be an extremely favorable picture of female executives.

text: As we sought to understand why women fail to impress with their vision, research from prior studies was not much help. To begin with, most attempts to compare men’s and women’s styles have focused on how leaders are rated by subordinates. Yet, as we all know, leaders play a key role in dealing with people above, across, and outside their units. Moreover, the vast majority of studies ask participants either to rate hypothetical male and female leaders or to evaluate the ‘majority’ of male and female leaders they know, rather than the actual specific leaders they know well.

runs.text: As we sought to understand why women fail to impress with their vision, research from prior studies was not much help. To begin with, most attempts to compare men’s and women’s styles have focused on how leaders are rated by subordinates. Yet, as we all know, leaders play a key role in dealing with people above, across, and outside their units. Moreover, the vast majority of studies ask participants either to rate hypothetical male and female leaders or to evaluate the ‘majority’ of male and female leaders they know, rather than the actual specific leaders they know well.

text: We turned therefore to the experts who were living this reality every day: the women participating in our executive education programs. When we asked how they would interpret our data, we heard three explanations. First, several women noted that they tended to set strategy via processes that differed from those used by their male counterparts. One executive put it like this: ‘Many women tend to be quite collaborative in forming their vision. They take into account the input of many and then describe the result as the group’s vision rather than their own.’ This suggests that what may in fact be visionary leadership is not perceived that way because it takes a different path.

text: Second, we heard that women often find it risky to stray away from concrete facts, analyses, and details. Some women responded to our findings by noting that they need to base their orders on concrete facts, not unprovable assertions about how the future will take shape. One management consultant observed that ‘Men speak more confidently and boldly on an issue, with very little data to back it up. Women want to have a lot of data and feel confident that they can back up what they are saying.’

text: And third, many women betrayed negative attitudes toward visionary leadership. Because they thought of themselves as grounded and concrete and had seen many so-called visionary ideas come unstuck in execution, they tended to eye envisioning behavior with some suspicion. Our interviews with female executives highlighted one potential difference in attitude between the genders that could explain women’s lower ratings on envisioning. We suspect women may not regard envisioning as a critical leadership competency to the same extent that men do. Over and over again in our discussions with women, we heard them take pride in their concrete no-nonsense attitude toward everyday work problems.

text: Women may dismiss the importance of vision, but the fact remains that women are a minority in the top ranks of business organizations. Our findings suggest that the shortfall is due in no small part to women’s perceived lack of vision. The findings of a 2008 study by researchers Jeanine Prime and Nancy Carter and Professors Karsten Jonsen and Martha Maznevski concur. In it, more than 1,000 executives from nine countries were asked for their impression of men and women as leaders. Both men and women tended to believe that the two genders have distinct leadership strengths, with women outscoring men on some behaviors and men outscoring women on others. But here’s the catch: When people were asked to rate the behaviors’ relative importance to overall leadership effectiveness, the ‘male’ behaviors had the edge. Across all countries, ‘inspiring others’ – a component of the envisioning dimension – was rated as most important to overall leadership effectiveness. And the ‘female’ skill of ‘supporting others’ ranked at the bottom of the list; it was clearly not critical but merely nice to have. The challenge facing women, then, is to stop dismissing the vision phenomenon and make vision one of the things they are known for. Of all the leadership dimensions we measured, it’s the only thing holding women back.
